reason: The allowed perfectness and orientation facts leave a concrete, nonroutine obstruction to two comparability covers. One must relate row middle points in two independent partial orders, force a monochromatic column triangle in the opposite order, and then use its middle vertex and a pendant edge. This interaction supports H2. The finite count and the perfectness certification alone would not support that grade; I find no additional H3-level core after the stated prerequisites.
core_assessment: I read source637-638, the entire proof642-701 and the listed definitions before seeing the selector difficulty fields. Rows are four cliques of size9 and columns are nine cliques of size4. A row vertex with no incoming-and-outgoing pair in either cover can be assigned one of four extremal status pairs. Two vertices assigned the same pair cannot share an edge in A or in B, contradicting the row clique, so there are at most4 bad vertices per row. Thus at least20 vertices are good; with nine columns, some column has at least3 good vertices. If u is A-good in its row, every column edge uv to another row is forbidden in A: either orientation combines with one of the two row-path edges to force a nonexistent diagonal edge. This holds even when A and B overlap and even when their orientations disagree on a shared edge. Consequently column vertices good for opposite covers cannot coexist. Nor can one of these three vertices be good for both covers, since its edge to either other vertex would belong to neither cover. All three therefore have the same good type; their three connecting edges belong exclusively to the other cover. A transitive orientation of this triangle has a middle vertex v. That vertex lies in directed two-edge paths for both covers. Whichever cover contains the pendant edge at v, either orientation of that edge forces a second neighbor of its leaf. The contradiction proves c(H)>=3. The disjoint row-edge, column-edge and matching-edge classes are each comparability graphs and partition E(H), proving p(H)<=3. Bipartite-line-graph perfectness and preservation under adding leaves give the remaining assertion.
prerequisite_assessment: The assumed characterization by transitive orientations is used separately in A and B; no edge-partition assumption enters the lower bound. Bipartite-line-graph perfectness and leaf preservation certify only perfectness, not the cover obstruction. Pigeonhole is used only after the four extremal types have been bounded. No local theorem or lower-bound result is hidden in the prerequisite list.

standard_prerequisites.name: Transitive orientations characterize comparability graphs
standard_prerequisites.statement: An orientation is transitive when u->v and v->w imply that uw is an edge and is oriented u->w. Comparability graphs are exactly graphs admitting such an orientation.
standard_prerequisites.use: Each covering comparability graph carries its own transitive orientation; an edge belonging to both is allowed two orientations.

standard_prerequisites.name: Bipartite line graphs are perfect
standard_prerequisites.statement: Every induced subgraph of the line graph of a bipartite graph has chromatic number equal to clique number, by the classical bipartite edge-coloring theorem. Attaching pendant vertices preserves perfectness.
standard_prerequisites.use: Certify only perfectness of the explicit grid-with-leaves graph. No lower bound on the cover parameter is assumed.

standard_prerequisites.name: Elementary finite pigeonhole principle
standard_prerequisites.use: Convert four types of bad row vertices into three good vertices in one column after the nontrivial local orientation constraints are established.

core_obligations: Separate edge cover from partition, allowing overlap and independent orientations in two hypothetical covers.
Classify vertices that are not a middle point of a directed length-two path in either row orientation by four extremal types, and prove each type occurs at most once in a row.
Show that good vertices in one column must have the same row-orientation type and all column edges between them must lie exclusively in the other cover, since diagonal grid edges do not exist.
Force one vertex to be the middle of directed paths for both orientations and use its pendant edge to contradict transitivity in whichever cover contains that edge.
Construct the three-cover partition explicitly from row cliques, column cliques and pendant edges.

proof_roadmap.step: Identify grid rows, columns and pendant edges; perfectness is classical and these three edge classes give a comparability partition.
Assume two possibly overlapping transitive covers; at most four bad vertices per nine-vertex row, hence one four-vertex column contains three good vertices.
Nonexistent diagonal edges force all three row types to agree and the column triangle into the other orientation. Its middle vertex has no allowable pendant orientation in either cover.
